title: Haryana Destroys 50,000 Kg of Adulterated Sweets and Fake Paneer Before Diwali
excerpt: A statewide drive launched on October 1 collected 1,288 samples, with more than 170 failing laboratory tests and 30 declared unsafe, days before Diwali on November 8.
body:
• Haryana food safety authorities have destroyed about 50,000 kg of adulterated sweets and fake paneer in a statewide drive launched on October 1 ahead of Diwali.
  • Officials collected 1,288 samples during the drive; more than 170 failed laboratory tests and 30 were declared unsafe for consumption.
  • The manufacture and sale of analogue paneer are prohibited, and sweet shops must disclose the type of fat used in their products.
  • For shoppers buying mithai for Diwali on November 8: buy from reliable sellers, check packaging and expiry details, and report suspected adulteration to the state food safety authorities.

Haryana food safety authorities have destroyed about 50,000 kg of adulterated sweets and fake paneer in a statewide crackdown launched on October 1, according to a Times of India report summarised by Feedzop. The drive, run ahead of Diwali on November 8, collected 1,288 samples, of which more than 170 failed laboratory tests and 30 were declared unsafe for consumption.

The figure is a statewide total, and it is substantially larger than the individual seizures reported earlier in the festive season. In Gurugram, officials destroyed about 125 kg of foul-smelling paneer on October 26 and collected eight samples of paneer, khoa and sweets for testing, as covered in our earlier report on Haryana's Diwali sweet checks. The new tally puts the full scale of the October drive on record for the first time.

How the drive is being run

Joint teams are conducting raids and checking vehicles at state borders, according to the report. Names of vendors whose samples failed are being published online to inform consumers. Laboratories are prioritising analysis of festive-season samples within 48 hours, supported by five mobile testing units carrying out on-the-spot checks.

Two product rules are being enforced alongside the sampling. The manufacture and sale of analogue paneer — a lookalike product made without milk — are strictly prohibited, and sweet shops must disclose the type of fat used in their products, the report said.

The surveillance order behind it

The seizures follow a state order to intensify surveillance for Diwali and Chhath Puja. Health Minister Arti Singh Rao directed the Food and Drug Administration to collect 100 to 150 additional surveillance samples in each district, with district-level teams supervised by deputy commissioners inspecting major markets, sweet shops, dairies and milk vendors, FDA Commissioner Dr Manoj Kumar said in a statement reported by 5 Dariya News.

The same statement gives the baseline the festive drive builds on: between April 1 and September 30, 2026, Haryana food safety officers collected 2,428 samples — 1,239 enforcement samples and 1,189 surveillance samples — and laboratory analysis found 232 enforcement samples and 149 surveillance samples did not conform to prescribed standards. Action in those cases was initiated under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, the commissioner said.

Special attention in the festive campaign is on sweets, milk, paneer, khoya and ghee, the products whose consumption rises sharply at Diwali. Headquarters officials have also been directed to upload district-wise data on substandard and unsafe samples to the state portal every week.

What shoppers should do

The health minister appealed to the public to remain vigilant while purchasing food, buy only from reliable sources, and report any suspected adulteration or food safety activity to the concerned authorities, according to the FDA statement. That advice matches the guidance officials gave in Gurugram: check packaging and expiry details where they apply, and avoid sweets or dairy with an unusual smell, colour or texture.

Inspections are continuing across the state in the final days before Diwali, and vendors whose samples failed face action under the Food Safety and Standards Act once laboratory reports are complete.
